lesson.title: Getter Methods: Reading a Private Attribute Safely
lesson.summary: A getter is a method whose only job is to hand back the current value of an attribute, giving outside code a clear, intentional way to read data that's been marked private by convention.
lesson.body:
Once an attribute like self.__balance is name mangled, outside code can't casually read wallet.__balance the way it could read a plain public attribute, and that's the point: it discourages careless direct access. But objects still need to share their data with the rest of the program somehow, a wallet balance that no code anywhere can ever read isn't useful to anyone. The standard solution is a getter method: a small method whose entire job is to return the current value of a private attribute, on purpose, through a name that makes the intent obvious.

```python
class Wallet:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.__balance = balance

    def get_balance(self):
        return self.__balance

w = Wallet(250)
print(w.get_balance())
# Output: 250
```

Here, __init__ stores 250 into self.__balance, which, as you now know, is really stored under the mangled name _Wallet__balance. Because get_balance is defined inside the Wallet class body, the reference to self.__balance inside it is mangled the exact same way, so it correctly finds and returns that same 250. Calling w.get_balance() from outside the class works perfectly, print(w.get_balance()) prints 250, because get_balance is the class's own deliberately provided doorway to that data, rather than an accidental collision with the mangled name.

A getter like this is a small piece of code, but it buys you something real: a single, named, easy-to-find place where reading happens. If you ever needed to log every time someone checks a balance, or round it before displaying it, get_balance is the one place you'd change, instead of hunting down every spot in a large program that touches the attribute directly. It's also worth knowing, without needing to master it yet, that Python offers a special @property decorator that lets a method like this be accessed using plain attribute syntax, wallet.balance instead of wallet.get_balance(), while still running your code underneath. That's a refinement for a later lesson; the explicit getter method above is the foundational pattern, and it works correctly in every version of Python.
